description_en: The bridge is built accross the Tīlā Nadī (a tributary of the Karṇālī river), south of the village of Śrī Ḍhuskā and north-west of the locality of Khalnā (or Khallā).Traditional bridges of the Karṇālī region follow a construction principle similar to that of other cantilever bridges seen elsewhere in the Himalayas. Nevertheless, Karṇālī bridges, known in Khaśa language assãgu, stand appart for their large dimensions (up to 35 meters long,Andolfatto 2019) and unique ornamentation. Materials used for the construction are restricted to stone and wood. Nails are inserted in a few plancks, at each end of the bridge. These nails have no architetonic role but bear an apotropaic value: they ward off malevolent activities that could obstruct the river crossing.On each side, the bridge rests on a stone abutment. In this case the abutments were reinforced with gabion walls. Long wooden beams are inserted from the medium height of the abutments. In this case four levels of protruding beams are placed on top of each other, with stones insterted in between. Two pairs of large wooden pillars are placed on each end and each side of the bridge. Beams are placed between each pair of pillars, thus supporting the long struts protruding from the abutments. The transverse displacement of some sleepers is prevented by inserting large wooden keys at the level of the perpendicular beams placed between the pillars.On top, the bridge deck is composed of long and thick plancks. Side plancks are placed vertically on each side of the deck to form parapets. The large pillars protrude over the deck. Although these elements are often richly carved, in the case of the Khalnā Sãgu carvings are limited to piled up rounded shapes.According to local informants (interviewed in 2018) this bridge is approximately thirty-forty years old. It is used daily, by pedestrians, motorcycles and cattle.
references: REFERENCES Andolfatto, David C. Le Pays aux Cent-Vingt-Cinq-Mille Montagnes. Etude Archéologique du Bassin de la Karnali (Népal) entre le XIIe et le XVIe siècle . Paris: Sorbonne University, 2019.
